problem: Vision-language navigation systems such as LM-Nav rely on CLIP embeddings whose space lacks robust semantics, but nobody had studied how this can be exploited to hijack the routes these systems plan.
motivation: VLN systems built on frozen foundation models are moving toward real robots and driving. Imperceptible image edits can change CLIP representations drastically, so stored map images could be silently tampered with to send a robot to a malicious destination. Defenses are needed too.
key_idea: Use gradient-based embedding alignment to make a minimal set of graph-node images match landmark text (or push others away via a low-similarity image) so LM-Nav's planner follows an attacker-chosen route, and detect the edits via their high sensitivity to small Gaussian noise.
insight: Embedding alignment yields near-invisible modifications (image-to-image PSNR 42.86 dB, SSIM 0.975; image-to-text PSNR 40.45 dB, SSIM 0.962) that fully change CLIP representations, so a 100% route modification rate is reached. Arrival success drops to 30% in the small environment because LM-Nav sums similarities across landmarks, so earlier optimized nodes can outweigh the target node. Adversarial images are far more sensitive to tiny Gaussian noise (std 1e-5) than natural ones, which gives 0.963 detection accuracy.
method: Threat model: attacker edits stored images in LM-Nav's topological graph (front/back views per node), leaving the planner and models untouched
Node selection (Alg. 1): Dijkstra shortest path from start to malicious target, then a DP over path nodes and landmark text embeddings (O(m*n)) picks the nodes already most similar to each landmark
Embedding alignment: minimize 0.5*||f(x0+dx)-f(x_tg)||^2 by gradient descent on the input image, with text or image targets, 12,000 steps, until L2 and cosine thresholds are met

Node modification (Alg. 2): raise chosen nodes' similarity to their landmark text; for any other node scoring higher on that landmark, align it to the lowest-similarity image in the graph to suppress it
Detection: compare CLIP embeddings of an image with and without Gaussian noise (std ~1e-5); adversarial images show a larger feature difference (threshold 0.203)

setting.backbone: LM-Nav (GPT-3 LLM + CLIP ViT-L/14 VLM + ViNT-style VNM), pretrained and frozen
setting.training_data: none (attack via per-image gradient optimization; no model training)
setting.observation: RECON dataset topological graphs, front and back monocular RGB images per node plus GPS
setting.action_space: graph node traversal (LM-Nav topological route planning)
setting.simulator: none; offline RECON real-robot dataset graphs (EnvLarge-10, EnvSmall-10)
setting.privileged: White-box access to CLIP weights and the stored graph images, and knowledge of the landmarks and target node

numbers.extra: attack: 12,000 optimization steps per image; white-box CLIP

the detection task achieved an accuracy of 0.963 and an F1 score of 0.961 for a balanced sample set of 278 nodes

numbers_note: No standard VLN benchmark is used; results are on the authors' own attack metrics over 20 LM-Nav graph paths. Detection accuracy and F1 are printed as fractions (0.963, 0.961). Image-quality numbers: PSNR 42.86 dB and SSIM 0.975 for image-to-image, and PSNR 40.45 dB and SSIM 0.962 for image-to-text.
results: The attack diverted routes in all 20 paths (100% route modification), reaching the malicious node 90% of the time in EnvLarge-10 and 30% in EnvSmall-10. Modifications stay near-invisible (PSNR about 40-43 dB, SSIM about 0.96-0.98). The noise-sensitivity detector reaches 0.963 accuracy. There are no baseline attacks to compare against.
limitations: Evaluated only on LM-Nav with CLIP ViT-L/14 and 20 paths over 2 graphs; white-box access is assumed and the attack is offline (edits to stored images, no physical-world attack)
Arrival success is low (30%) in the small environment because LM-Nav sums similarities across landmarks, so earlier optimized nodes can win
The detector's noise range may vary across datasets, and adaptive attackers are not considered
